why_angle: West Electric's comparison gives only capacity. It says a battery without solar 'can only ride out a single outage cycle' and mentions 'native generator integration' with no figures. No rival page gives how fast a grid-charged battery refills during an outage, what generator does it, how much fuel it burns, or that the E10 holds a 240 V portable generator near 20 A until the app setting is changed. This page sizes the refill.

page.title: Whole House Battery Backup Without Solar: 4 Kits Compared by How They Refill
page.h1: Whole house battery backup without solar: the kits that keep going after the first charge
page.desc: Without solar, a home battery charges from the grid. We compare four kits by runtime, grid charging and how each refills during a long outage.
page.answer: Short answer. A whole house battery backup without solar relies on grid charging, so in a long outage it needs a generator to refill. Best kit: Anker SOLIX E10 with two batteries, Power Dock and Smart Generator 5500, whose generator refills the 12.3 kWh in about 2.7 hours.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Runtime. The average US home buys 10,791 kWh a year (EIA, 2022). 10,791 ÷ 365 = 29.6 kWh a day, or 1.23 kW on average. 12.288 kWh ÷ 1.23 kW ≈ 10 h. 24.576 kWh ÷ 1.23 kW ≈ 20 h. 5.53 kWh ÷ 1.23 kW ≈ 4.5 h. Central AC or electric heat shortens these; running only essentials lengthens them.
  • Refill during an outage. 12.288 kWh ÷ 4.5 kW ≈ 2.7 h from the Smart Generator 5500. The generator's own spec table lists 3,600 W DC, which gives 12.288 ÷ 3.6 ≈ 3.4 h. Quiet mode runs at 2 kW: 12.288 ÷ 2 ≈ 6.1 h.
  • Fuel. Anker rates one 2.64 gal tank at about 17 kWh. 29.6 kWh a day ÷ 17 kWh ≈ 1.74 tanks, or about 4.6 gal of gasoline a day for an average home.
  • Grid charging. At 240 V the E10 takes 7,680 W: 12.288 ÷ 7.68 ≈ 1.6 h. On a 120 V outlet it takes at most 1,800 W.
  • Generator vs more battery. Two more B6000 modules cost $4,000 and add 12.288 kWh, used once per outage. The Smart Generator 5500 costs $1,600 as an E10 add-on and adds about 17 kWh per tank for as long as there is fuel.
  • BLUETTI usable energy. StorageReview measured 2.39 kWh delivered from one 2,764.8 Wh Apex 300 (86%) and 89% from a stack with two B300K. Grid charging through the P050A port runs up to 3,840 W: 5.53 ÷ 3.84 ≈ 1.4 h.
Your situationKit
Outages that last days, nobody wants to touch a switchNo solar, long outages
Same need, smaller budget, someone home to switch overLower cost, manual switchover
Generator not allowed, outages usually under a dayNo generator allowed
Only the fridge, lights and internet matterEssentials on a budget

{kit:kit-anker-e10-power-dock-generator} is the pick for most homes without solar. The Power Dock switches over in 20 ms or less and manages 12 circuits, which keeps the house inside the E10's 7,680 W. The generator then starts by itself when the battery falls to the level you set and stops when the battery is full. Anker also lists an E10 + Power Dock + Smart Generator 5500 bundle at $7,399. Its box list names a B6000, but the same page sells the B6000 as a separate $2,000 add-on, so check that the cart shows two batteries before you pay.

{kit:kit-anker-e10-inlet-box-generator} uses the same battery and generator with the Smart Inlet Box instead of the Power Dock, for $1,500 less. The trade: switchover is manual (the E10 manual has you lock the main breaker with an interlock), Anker's comparison page lists no smart-load control, and the inlet box needs a 40 A breaker on the grid port and a 50 A breaker on the off-grid port.

{kit:kit-anker-e10-4-battery-no-generator} is for homes where a generator isn't an option. It doubles the stored energy to about 20 hours of average use, but once the battery is empty the house is dark until the grid returns.

{kit:kit-bluetti-apex-300-essentials} costs about a third as much, but its 3,840 W and 5.53 kWh cover essential circuits rather than the whole house. BLUETTI says the Apex 300 is expected to ship in late January.

How a battery without solar refills when the grid is down

Without solar, a home battery charges from the grid. During a long outage the only way to refill it is a generator, and the generator's charging rate decides how long the battery keeps the house running.

  • Anker's own generator. The Smart Generator 5500 connects to the E10 over a dedicated power-and-data cable and puts in 4,500 W DC on gasoline or LPG, or 4,000 W on natural gas (Anker). Anker notes that most third-party portable generators lack auto-start by the battery's charge level or from the app.
  • A 240 V portable generator you already own. Ken Yannacci at EV Outdoors charged the E10 at 240 V from a Silverado EV and saw the input held to about 20 A (4,800 W) until he changed the running wattage under AC Input Settings → 240 V Portable Generator in the Anker app. He advises not exceeding 80% of the source's rating: the Silverado EV's 7,200 W × 0.8 = 5,760 W. At 4,800 W a 12.288 kWh refill takes 12.288 ÷ 4.8 ≈ 2.6 h.
  • A 120 V generator. The E10 takes at most 1,800 W at 120 V, and Anker says charging above 12 A should run for less than 3 hours at a time. Plan on 12 A × 120 V = 1,440 W: 12.288 ÷ 1.44 ≈ 8.5 h.
  • Power quality. The E10 manual calls for third-party AC generators with total harmonic distortion under 10%. Champion lists its inverter generators at 3% THD or less.
  • Standby generators and the house. The Power Dock works only on 120/240 V split-phase service with a main breaker of 200 A or less (Power Dock manual). Anker says standby generators on the Power Dock must be 240 V models with Two Wire or Utility Sensing control and no more than 24 kW surge, and that the battery doesn't power the home while a standby generator runs.
